mainTopic: Idolatrous intent in שחיטה: the unresolved incident in קיסרי, הוכיח סופו על תחילתו, and the ruling like רבי יוסי
overview: The amud opens with the end of a קל וחומר: in חולין, only the slaughterer's intent counts. A ברייתא then supports רבי יוחנן, ruling that slaughtering in order to sprinkle the blood or burn the fat for עבודה זרה makes the animal זבחי מתים. In a case in קיסרי, the idolatrous thought came only after the slaughter, and the חכמים gave no ruling. רב חסדא says they were silent out of respect for both the רבנן and רבי אליעזר, but the גמרא shows that the case may not depend on their מחלוקת. רב שיזבי says instead that they did not permit the animal out of respect for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who holds הוכיח סופו על תחילתו. The גט case is tried as his source and rejected. רבינא then points to the ברייתא about slaves that the receiver refused, where רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says a later protest reveals his original refusal. The גמרא then rules like רבי יוסי that only the slaughterer's intent matters, applies this to Arabs who wanted the blood and fat, and discusses a גוי paying a זוז according to רבי אליעזר. A new משנה begins: slaughtering for the sake of mountains, seas and the like is invalid.

steps.title: Closing the argument: in non-sacred animals, only the slaughterer's intent counts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes a קל וחומר: in חולין, intent can only disqualify during two acts, so surely everything depends only on the one who slaughters.
steps.simpleTranslation: In non-sacred animals, intent disqualifies during only two acts. Isn't it logical, then, that everything should follow only the intent of the slaughterer?
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of a קל וחומר that started before this section. It concludes that with חולין, only the slaughterer's thoughts matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument compares חולין to קדשים. In קדשים, intent has power over more acts, yet we still follow only the person doing the act. Since in חולין intent works in only two acts, it is all the more reasonable to follow only the slaughterer.

keyTerms.meaning: Intent or thought while doing the act, which can disqualify it
Disqualifies or invalidates
Ordinary, non-sacred animals
Is it not logical? This is the closing phrase of a קל וחומר

steps.confusionAlert: This line is the second half of a sentence. The first half, about קדשים, came before this section, so don't read it as a brand-new statement.

phrases.english: then in a place where intent does not invalidate in non-sacred animals
except during two acts of service,
phrases.notes: The two acts are slaughtering and sprinkling the blood.

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ דִּין שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא הַכֹּל הוֹלֵךְ
phrases.english: is it not logical that everything should go
only after the slaughterer?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵינוֹ דִּין שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא הַכֹּל הוֹלֵךְ אֶלָּא אַחַר הַשּׁוֹחֵט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a קל וחומר that began before this section
steps.raayaObject: Only the slaughterer's intent determines the status of a חולין slaughter
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר from the laws of intent in קדשים

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבי יוחנן, and tells of the incident in קיסרי
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that slaughtering in order to sprinkle the blood or burn the fat for עבודה זרה makes the animal forbidden. If the thought came only after the slaughter, there was a real case in קיסרי where the חכמים gave no ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא supports רבי יוחנן. If someone slaughters an animal in order to sprinkle its blood or burn its fat for idol worship, these are offerings to the dead. If he slaughtered it and only afterward had that idolatrous intent, this happened in קיסרי, and the חכמים said neither 'forbidden' nor 'permitted' about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up רבי יוחנן. Intent during the slaughter about a later idolatrous act makes the animal forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case matches רבי יוחנן: a thought during slaughter about a future act (sprinkling or burning) already ruins the animal. The second case is different, because the bad thought came only after the slaughter was done. For that case the חכמים refused to decide either way, which sets up רב חסדא's explanation in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: In agreement with him, supporting his view
Offerings to the dead, meaning sacrifices to idols, which are forbidden
To burn its fat, as is done on an altar
Neither forbidden nor permitted, meaning no ruling was given

steps.whyThisMatters: The silence of the חכמים in the Caesarea case becomes the focus of the rest of the sugya.

phrases.english: It is taught in a baraita in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan:
One who slaughters the animal
in order to sprinkle its blood for idol worship
or to burn its fat for idol worship,
these are offerings to the dead.
phrases.notes: The phrase comes from תהלים 106:28. 'The dead' means idols.

phrases.english: If he slaughtered it and afterward had intent about it,
this was an incident in Caesarea,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָמְרוּ בָּהּ לֹא אִיסּוּר וְלֹא הֶיתֵּר.
phrases.english: and they said about it neither prohibition nor permission.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא כְּוָותֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a תנאי source that supports רבי יוחנן's position in the sugya
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's view that intent during slaughter about a later idolatrous act forbids the animal
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא ruling that such an animal is זבחי מתים

steps.title: Why the חכמים stayed silent in קיסרי
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא explains that the חכמים did not forbid the animal out of respect for the רבנן, and did not permit it out of respect for רבי אליעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: They did not say it was forbidden, out of respect for the רבנן. They did not say it was permitted, out of respect for רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא explains the silence in the קיסרי case. He connects it to the מחלוקת in the משנה between the רבנן and רבי אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי אליעזר assumes an idol worshipper's unspoken intent is for idolatry, so he would forbid the animal. The רבנן do not assume this, so they would permit it. Because the קיסרי case seemed to depend on this מחלוקת, the חכמים did not want to rule against either side.

keyTerms.meaning: The honor of the רבנן, meaning out of respect for their opinion
His honor, meaning out of respect for that sage

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
They did not say prohibition about it
because of the honor of the Rabbis.
Not permission
because of the honor of Rabbi Eliezer.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא לֹא אָמְרוּ בָּהּ אִיסּוּר מִשּׁוּם כְּבוֹדָן דְּרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the silence of the חכמים in the Caesarea case from the ברייתא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Caesarea case depends on the מחלוקת between the רבנן and רבי אליעזר, so no ruling was given out of respect for both

steps.title: Challenge: maybe even the רבנן would forbid when the intent is heard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רב חסדא knows the case depends on the מחלוקת. Perhaps the רבנן permit only when we never heard any idolatrous intent, but here he said it, so his later words prove his earlier intent.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do you know this? Perhaps the רבנן said it is permitted only there in the משנה, because we did not hear him express idolatrous intent. But here, where we heard that he had such intent, his end proves what he meant at the beginning!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב חסדא. Perhaps even the רבנן would forbid the animal in the קיסרי case, so it would not depend on the מחלוקת at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the person never said anything, so the רבנן do not assume bad intent. In קיסרי, he openly showed idolatrous intent after the slaughter. That later intent might reveal that he meant it all along, so even the רבנן might agree it is forbidden, and there would be no reason to stay silent for their honor.

keyTerms.meaning: From where? How do you know?
Perhaps
They only said their view up to this point, meaning their rule is limited to that case
His end proves his beginning: later actions reveal what he intended earlier

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not saying the animal is definitely forbidden. It only shows that the Caesarea case might not depend on the מחלוקת, which weakens רב חסדא's explanation.

phrases.english: From where do you know this?

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמְרִי רַבָּנַן הָתָם,
phrases.english: Perhaps the Rabbis said their ruling only there,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the case in our משנה, where the slaughter was for an idol worshipper.

phrases.english: because we did not hear him that he had intent,
but here, where we heard him that he had intent,
his end proves his beginning!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִמַּאי דִּלְמָא עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמְרִי רַבָּנַן הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב חסדא's claim that the Caesarea case depends on the מחלוקת in the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's assumption that the רבנן would permit the animal in the Caesarea case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רבנן's leniency may apply only when no intent was expressed. When intent is expressed later, הוכיח סופו על תחילתו could make even the רבנן forbid it, so silence for their honor would be unnecessary.

steps.title: Maybe רבי אליעזר only spoke about a נכרי
steps.stepSummary: A second challenge to רב חסדא: perhaps רבי אליעזר forbids only when a נכרי is involved, because a נכרי's ordinary thoughts lean toward עבודה זרה. For a Jew, even רבי אליעזר would not say the end proves the beginning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or another possibility: רבי אליעזר only said his ruling there about a נכרי, because a נכרי's normal intention is for עבודה זרה. But with a Jew, we do not say that his later words prove what he meant at the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second way to show that the קיסרי case may not depend on the מחלוקת between רבי אליעזר and the רבנן, as רב חסדא claimed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 4 the גמרא said even the רבנן might forbid here. Now it says the opposite side: even רבי אליעזר might permit here. His strict ruling may apply only to a נכרי, whose usual thoughts are idolatrous, while the קיסרי animal belonged to a Jew.

keyTerms.meaning: Alternatively, or another possibility
The ordinary, unstated intention of a gentile
His end proves his beginning: later words or actions reveal earlier intent

steps.confusionAlert: This does not say רבי אליעזר disagrees with himself. It says his ruling may have been limited from the start to a case involving a נכרי.

phrases.english: Alternatively,

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר הָתָם
phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer only said his ruling there
phrases.notes: "There" means the משנה where רבי אליעזר rules about slaughtering on behalf of a gentile.

phrases.english: regarding a gentile,
since the ordinary thought of a gentile is for idol worship,
but with a Jew,

phrases.aramaic: הוֹכִיחַ סוֹפוֹ עַל תְּחִלָּתוֹ לָא אָמְרִינַן.
phrases.english: we do not say that his end proves his beginning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי, עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, parallel challenge to רב חסדא, this time limiting רבי אליעזר's view instead of the רבנן's.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's claim that the קיסרי case depends on the מחלוקת of רבי אליעזר and the רבנן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רבי אליעזר's strictness applies only to a נכרי, he would permit in the קיסרי case of a Jew, so there was no reason to hold back out of respect for him.

steps.title: רב שיזבי: no permission out of respect for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: רב שיזבי gives a new explanation. The חכמים did not permit the animal out of respect for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who holds that a person's later actions can reveal his earlier intent.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב שיזבי said: they did not declare the animal permitted out of respect for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.whatsHappening: Because רב חסדא's explanation was challenged, רב שיזבי offers a different reason why the חכמים in קיסרי did not permit the animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אלא shows that רב חסדא's approach is being set aside. Instead of linking the case to רבי אליעזר, רב שיזבי links it to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who reads a person's earlier intent from what he does later.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather: drops the previous approach and brings a new one
A ruling that something is permitted
Out of respect for him

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Sheizevi said:
They did not declare it permitted

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם כְּבוֹדוֹ דְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל,
phrases.english: out of respect for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב שֵׁיזְבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב חסדא's explanation after the two challenges in steps 4 and 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the explanation: the source of hesitation is a different תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case depends on רבי אליעזר versus the רבנן (רב חסדא)
steps.terutzMaskana: The חכמים held back from permitting because of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view that later actions reveal earlier intent

steps.title: Which teaching of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where we see that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds this view.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which teaching of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל is meant?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of רב שיזבי's claim. This sets up the next move, where it suggests a teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב שיזבי said we must respect רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's opinion, but he did not say where that opinion appears. The גמרא wants the specific teaching that shows he says the end proves the beginning.

keyTerms.meaning: Which?

phrases.english: Which teaching of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵי רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind רב שיזבי's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which ruling of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל shows that later actions reveal earlier intent

steps.title: Suggestion: his ruling about a גט
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the teaching is רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's ruling about divorce. It begins quoting the משנה: a healthy man who says "write a גט for my wife" is assumed to be just teasing her.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's ruling about a גט, as the משנה teaches: a healthy man who said "Write a גט for my wife" only wanted to mock her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible answer and starts quoting the משנה it has in mind. The word אילימא ("if you say") signals that this suggestion will be examined.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's background rule is that a healthy man's words "write a גט" are not treated as a real order to divorce, because he probably only meant to tease her. This prepares the story in the next step, where רבן שמעון בן גמליאל uses later actions to judge this kind of statement.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say: offers a suggestion that will be tested
A healthy person, as opposed to someone near death
A bill of divorce
To mock or tease her

phrases.aramaic: אִילֵּימָא רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל דְּגִיטִּין,
phrases.english: If you say it is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling about bills of divorce,
as we learned in a mishna:
A healthy man who said, "Write a bill of divorce for my wife"
only wanted to mock her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל דְּגִיטִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a possible answer to the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Possibly the ruling in the משנה in גיטין about a healthy man who orders a גט to be written

steps.title: The man who fell from the roof
steps.stepSummary: The משנה tells of a healthy man who ordered a גט written, then fell from a roof and died. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל rules: if he fell on purpose, the גט is valid. If the wind pushed him, it is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a case of a healthy man who said "Write a גט for my wife," then went up to the roof, fell, and died. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said: if he fell on his own, it is a valid גט. If the wind pushed him, it is not a valid גט.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the משנה. This story shows how רבן שמעון בן גמליאל seems to judge a person's earlier words by what he did afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the man threw himself off the roof, his act shows that he was already planning to die when he ordered the גט. So he meant it seriously, like a dying man. If the wind pushed him, his death tells us nothing about his earlier intent. This looks like "his end proves his beginning," which is what רב שיזבי needs.

keyTerms.meaning: An actual incident that happened
He fell on his own, on purpose
The wind pushed him

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the candidate source for רב שיזבי's claim that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל reads earlier intent from later actions.

phrases.english: And there was an incident with a healthy man who said,
"Write a bill of divorce for my wife,"
and he went up to the roof, fell, and died.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said:

phrases.aramaic: אִם מֵעַצְמוֹ נָפַל, הֲרֵי זֶה גֵּט,
phrases.english: If he fell on his own, it is a valid bill of divorce,
and if the wind pushed him, it is not a valid bill of divorce.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַעֲשֶׂה בְּבָרִיא שֶׁאָמַר כִּתְבוּ גֵּט לְאִשְׁתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the משנה quote begun in step 8 with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's actual ruling.
steps.raayaObject: That רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that later actions reveal earlier intent
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in גיטין about the healthy man who fell from the roof

steps.title: Does the story contradict the rule in the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls an old difficulty in the גט משנה: the story seems to go against the rule stated just before it.
steps.simpleTranslation: We discussed this משנה and asked: does the משנה bring a story that contradicts its own rule?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses on the גט משנה it just quoted and points out a problem in how it is written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה first says a healthy man who says 'write a גט' is only teasing his wife, so there is no גט. Then it tells a story where such a גט can be valid. A story is supposed to support the rule, not contradict it.

keyTerms.meaning: And we discussed it (we raised a question about this source)
A story brought to contradict? (a story should support the rule, not go against it)

phrases.english: And we discussed it:
Does it bring a story to contradict?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָוֵינַן בַּהּ: מַעֲשֶׂה לִסְתּוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises an internal difficulty in the משנה just quoted as the source for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The structure of the גט משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule says a healthy man's 'write a גט' is just teasing, yet the story shows a case where it is a valid גט.

steps.title: The משנה is missing a line: the end can prove the beginning
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is missing words. It really teaches that if the husband's later actions prove his first intent, the גט is valid, and the story illustrates this.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is missing words, and this is what it teaches: if his end proves his beginning, it is a valid גט. And there was also a story of a healthy man who said 'write a גט for my wife,' then went up to the roof, fell, and died. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said: if he fell on his own, it is a valid גט. If the wind pushed him, it is not a גט.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem by adding a missing line to the משנה, so the story now fits the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a healthy man saying 'write a גט' is just teasing. But the משנה adds an exception: if what he does later shows he really meant it, the גט is valid. Jumping off the roof shows he knew he would die and truly wanted the גט. Being blown off by the wind shows nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: It is missing words (the text needs a line added to be read correctly)
His end proved his beginning (later actions reveal earlier intent)
He fell on his own (on purpose)
The wind pushed him

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the idea that a person's end can reveal his beginning. The next step, though, rejects this גט case as the source the חכמים were respecting in the animal case.

phrases.english: It is missing words
and this is what it teaches:
if his end proved his beginning –
phrases.notes: This is the missing line. It comes right after the rule that a healthy man is just teasing.

phrases.english: If he fell on his own, it is a valid גט,
and if the wind pushed him, it is not a גט.

steps.triggerLanguage: חַסּוֹרֵי מִיחַסְּרָא וְהָכִי קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty of step 10 by adding a missing clause to the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adding a missing line to the text (חסורי מיחסרא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story contradicts the rule that a healthy man is only teasing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule has an exception: when his end proves his beginning, the גט is valid, and the story shows that exception.

steps.title: The גט case may be different because he said 'write'
steps.stepSummary: The proof from the גט case is pushed away: there the husband said 'write,' so he already showed some intent, unlike the animal case.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe it is different there, because he said 'write.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the גט משנה as the source that the חכמים were respecting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the גט case the husband actually gave an instruction, 'write a גט,' so his own words already point toward divorce, and his fall only confirms it. In the animal case, nothing he said at the start showed his intent. So the גט case does not prove that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל would let the end prove the beginning where there was no such statement.

keyTerms.meaning: But maybe (introduces a pushback)
It is different there
Write! (the husband's instruction)

phrases.english: But maybe it is different there,
because he said, 'Write.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִלְמָא שָׁאנֵי הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the identification of the גט משנה as the source of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The use of the גט משנה as the source for the respected view
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: In the גט case the husband's words 'write' already showed intent, which is missing in the animal case.

steps.title: רבינא points to a different teaching of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: רבינא agrees the חכמים held back out of respect for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, but says it was for a different teaching of his.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבינא said: it was out of respect for the teaching of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל found here.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers a new source for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view. This line sets up the ברייתא he is about to quote.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea from step 6 stays the same: the חכמים did not permit the animal out of respect for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. What changes is which teaching of his they were respecting. Instead of the גט case, רבינא points to the ברייתא that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: Out of respect for him
That is found here (the teaching about to be quoted)

phrases.english: Rather, Ravina said:
Out of respect for
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel of this teaching,
phrases.notes: He means the teaching he is about to quote, not the גט case.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the גט source was rejected, offers a new source for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing the source with a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The respected view is רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's ruling about the גט.
steps.terutzMaskana: The respected view is his ruling in the ברייתא about the slaves.

steps.title: The slaves the receiver did not want
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: a man gave property with slaves, and the receiver said 'I do not want them.' The תנא קמא says the slaves belong to the receiver, but רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the heirs already own them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: if someone writes his property over to others, and there were slaves in it, and that person said 'I do not want them,' then if their second master is a כהן, these slaves may eat תרומה. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: once that person said 'I do not want them,' the heirs have already acquired them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא quotes the ברייתא that shows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the תנא קמא, the receiver already owns the slaves, so if he is a כהן they eat תרומה even though he refused them. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says his refusal shows he never took them, so they went to the heirs. His later words reveal what was true from the start, which is the view the חכמים respected.

keyTerms.meaning: One who writes his property over to others
I do not want them
Their second master (the person receiving them)
They may eat תרומה (as slaves of a כהן)
The heirs acquired them

steps.whatToRemember: רבינא's source for 'the end reveals the beginning' is the slaves ברייתא: by refusing, the receiver shows he never owned them, so the heirs did all along.
steps.confusionAlert: The 'second master' is not the giver. He is the person receiving the slaves, and the תרומה question depends on whether he is a כהן.

phrases.english: As it was taught: One who writes his property over to others,
and there were slaves among it,
and that person said, 'I do not want them,'
phrases.notes: 'That person' is the one receiving the property.

phrases.english: if their second master was a כהן –
these may eat תרומה.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Once that person said, 'I do not want them' –
the heirs have already acquired them.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: הַכּוֹתֵב נְכָסָיו לַאֲחֵרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the ברייתא that רבינא's statement refers to.
steps.raayaObject: That רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds a person's later words or actions can reveal what was true from the start
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about property with slaves that the receiver refused

steps.title: Does the receiver really acquire even while protesting?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls an old difficulty with the תנא קמא's view: can a person really be forced to own slaves while he is shouting that he does not want them?
steps.simpleTranslation: We once asked about this ברייתא: according to the תנא קמא, does the receiver get the slaves even if he stands there shouting that he doesn't want them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reopens an older discussion on the ברייתא from Step 14. It points out that the תנא קמא's ruling sounds unreasonable, which sets up the answer coming next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא said the slaves belong to the receiver even though he said 'I do not want them.' But a gift is a favor, and you can't force a favor on someone who loudly refuses. So the גמרא needs to explain exactly which case the תנא קמא meant.

keyTerms.meaning: And we discussed it: the גמרא is recalling a question it raised earlier on this source
The first, unnamed opinion in a משנה or ברייתא
Shouts in protest; here, loudly refusing the gift

phrases.english: And we discussed it:
phrases.notes: 'It' is the ברייתא about the gift of slaves from Step 14.

phrases.english: According to the first tanna, does he acquire even if he stands and shouts?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָוֵינַן בַּהּ: לְתַנָּא קַמָּא, אֲפִילּוּ עוֹמֵד וְצוֹוֵחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a logical difficulty on the ברייתא just quoted in Step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling of the תנא קמא that the slaves belong to the receiver.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It makes no sense to force ownership on someone who loudly refuses it.

steps.title: Two cases where everyone agrees
steps.stepSummary: רבה (or רבי יוחנן) explains that in two cases there is no argument. Protest at the start means no acquisition. Silence followed by protest only later means he acquired.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said, and some say it was רבי יוחנן: If he protests right from the start, everyone agrees he did not acquire. If he was silent and only protested at the end, everyone agrees he did acquire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins to answer the question by setting aside two cases that both sides agree on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Protesting right away stops the gift, even for the תנא קמא. Staying silent when the gift reaches you counts as accepting it, so a later protest is too late, even for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. This narrows the argument down to a special in-between case.

keyTerms.meaning: From the start
Everyone agrees; there is no argument here
He acquired; the item legally became his
Is silent

phrases.english: Rabba said, and some say it was Rabbi Yoḥanan:
Where he shouts in protest from the start,

phrases.aramaic: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דְּלָא קָנָה,
phrases.english: everyone agrees that he did not acquire;
where he is silent and at the end shouts,
everyone agrees that he acquired.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר רַבָּה, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: בְּצוֹוֵחַ מֵעִיקָּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the difficulty of Step 15 by ruling out the obvious cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: the argument is not about these two cases.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The תנא קמא forces the gift even on someone protesting right away.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone agrees that an immediate protest blocks the gift and that a late protest after silence does not.

steps.title: The real argument: a gift given through someone else
steps.stepSummary: The argument is when someone else took the gift on his behalf. He was silent at first and protested later. The תנא קמא says his silence already made him the owner, so the protest is just backing out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where they argue is when the giver transferred the slaves to him through another person, and he was silent and later protested. The תנא קמא holds: since he was silent, he acquired them, and his protest now is just him backing out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא identifies the exact case of the argument and explains the תנא קמא's reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the gift came to him through a middleman, and he only protested when the slaves actually arrived. The תנא קמא reads his early silence as acceptance. Once he owns them, a later protest cannot undo the gift; it is just a change of mind.

keyTerms.meaning: Where they do argue
Transferred ownership to him through another person
He backs out; he changes his mind

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with the case in Step 16. There the gift came straight to him and he stayed silent. Here a middleman took it for him, and he protested once the slaves actually reached him.

phrases.english: Where they argue
is where he transferred ownership to him through another person,
and he was silent, and in the end he shouted.
The first tanna holds: since he was silent, he acquired them,

phrases.aramaic: וְהַאי דְּקָא צָוַוח – מִיהְדָּר קָא הָדַר בֵּיהּ.
phrases.english: and the fact that he is shouting means he is backing out.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי – שֶׁזִּיכָּה לוֹ עַל יְדֵי אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבה's answer by naming the case they argue about and explaining the תנא קמא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Setting the case: the argument is limited to a gift taken through a middleman.
steps.terutzMaskana: The תנא קמא never forces a gift on someone protesting from the start. He only treats early silence as acceptance.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: the end shows what he meant from the start
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that his final protest proves he never wanted the slaves. He stayed quiet earlier only because they had not reached him yet.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds: his ending proves his beginning. The reason he didn't protest at first is that he thought: as long as they haven't come into my hands, why should I protest?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבה's answer by explaining רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's side of the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, the early silence was not acceptance. It made sense to wait until the slaves actually arrived. So his protest at the end shows what he wanted all along, and the slaves stay with the giver's heirs.

keyTerms.meaning: His ending proves his beginning: later actions reveal his original intent
Into my hands; into my actual possession

steps.whatToRemember: The whole argument is about one case: a gift taken through a middleman, silence at first, protest when the slaves arrive. The תנא קמא says the silence was acceptance and the protest is backing out. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says הוכיח סופו על תחילתו, the same idea we saw with the גט in Steps 10-11.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the teaching of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל that רבינא pointed to in Step 13. Here too, a person's later behavior can reveal what he intended at the start.

phrases.english: And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds:
his ending proves his beginning,
and the fact that he did not shout from the start
is because he thought: as long as they have not come into my hands,
why should I shout?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל סָבַר: הוֹכִיחַ סוֹפוֹ עַל תְּחִילָּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the argument laid out in Step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why early silence does not count as acceptance for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, the later protest reveals his original refusal, so he never acquired the slaves.

steps.title: The הלכה follows רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, in the name of שמואל, rules that the הלכה follows רבי יוסי: the slaughterer's intention decides, not the owner's.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: the הלכה follows רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the argument in the משנה about slaughtering for a גוי and gives a final ruling: we follow רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי אליעזר says the owner's intention can ruin the שחיטה, so a Jew slaughtering for a גוי makes it פסול. רבי יוסי says everything follows the person doing the slaughtering. שמואל rules like רבי יוסי, so what the גוי owner has in mind does not ruin the שחיטה.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical law follows (this opinion)
Intention or thought during the שחיטה
The person doing the slaughtering

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling is the basis for the practical case in the next steps.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
The halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה's argument between רבי אליעזר and רבי יוסי and decides it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In slaughtering for a גוי, the הלכה follows רבי יוסי: only the slaughterer's intention matters.

steps.title: Arabs give rams and want the blood and fat
steps.stepSummary: Arabs in ציקוניא gave rams to Jewish slaughterers and kept the blood and fat for themselves. רב טובי בר רב מתנה asks רב יוסף what the law is.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some Arabs came to ציקוניא and gave rams to Jewish slaughterers. They said: the blood and fat are ours, the hide and meat are yours. רב טובי בר רב מתנה sent the question to רב יוסף: what is the law in a case like this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real story and asks a practical question. It is setting up רב יוסף's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Arabs clearly wanted the blood and fat for their idol worship, so the owners had a forbidden intention. The question is whether their intention ruins the Jewish slaughterer's שחיטה, which would make the meat forbidden to the Jews.

keyTerms.meaning: Arabs (desert traders)
Jewish slaughterers or butchers
The blood and the fat
The hide and the meat
In a case like this, what is the law?

phrases.english: There were these Arabs who came to Tzikuneya,
and they gave rams to Jewish slaughterers.
They said to them:
The blood and the fat are for us,
phrases.notes: They wanted these parts for their idol worship.

phrases.english: the hide and the meat are for you.

phrases.aramaic: שַׁלְחַהּ רַב טוֹבִי בַּר רַב מַתְנָה
phrases.english: Rav Tuvi bar Rav Mattana sent the question
before Rav Yosef:
In a case like this, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הַאי גַּוְונָא מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real-life case that tests the ruling of step 19.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the Arab owners' idol-worship intention ruin the Jewish slaughterer's שחיטה?

steps.title: רב יוסף answers with שמואל's ruling
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers by quoting שמואל's ruling that the הלכה follows רבי יוסי, so the שחיטה is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: He sent back: this is what רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל, the הלכה follows רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers the question by quoting the ruling from step 19.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since only the slaughterer's intention counts, the Arabs' plan for the blood and fat does not matter. The Jewish slaughterers had no forbidden intention, so the meat is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: He sent (an answer) back to him
Idol worship
So, like this

steps.whatToRemember: With a גוי owner, the Jewish slaughterer's intention decides. The owner's plan for idol worship does not ruin the שחיטה.

phrases.english: He sent to him:

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: This is what Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
The halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ: הָכִי אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The שחיטה is valid, because the הלכה follows רבי יוסי that the slaughterer's intention decides.

steps.title: For רבי אליעזר, what if a גוי pays a small coin?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב אויא asks רב אשי: according to רבי אליעזר, what if a גוי gives a Jewish slaughterer a זוז to buy a little of the meat?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא son of רב אויא said to רב אשי: according to רבי אליעזר, if a גוי gave a זוז to a Jewish slaughterer, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא asks a question about the other opinion, רבי אליעזר. It sets up רב אשי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר holds that slaughtering for a גוי makes the שחיטה פסול. The question is whether a small share, bought with one coin, counts as slaughtering for the גוי and ruins the whole animal.

keyTerms.meaning: A זוז, a small silver coin
Slaughterer or butcher
What (is the law)?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha, son of Rav Avya, said to Rav Ashi:
According to Rabbi Eliezer,

phrases.aramaic: יְהֵיב לֵיהּ זוּזָא לְטַבָּח יִשְׂרָאֵל, מַאי?
phrases.english: if [a gentile] gave a zuz to a Jewish slaughterer, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The coin pays for a small piece of the meat.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר, יְהֵיב לֵיהּ זוּזָא לְטַבָּח יִשְׂרָאֵל, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רבי יוסי's view to a question about רבי אליעזר's view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: According to רבי אליעזר, does a גוי's small paid share make the whole שחיטה count as being for him?

steps.title: It depends on whether the Jew can refuse him
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers: if the גוי is violent and cannot be refused, the animal is forbidden. If not, the Jew can simply send him away.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: we look at the situation. If he is a violent man whom the Jew cannot push away, it is forbidden. If not, the Jew can tell him, "Your head and a mountain!"
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers that it depends on the kind of person the גוי is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Jew cannot refuse a violent גוי, he is really slaughtering partly for the גוי, so for רבי אליעזר the animal is forbidden. If the Jew could easily refuse him, the coin does not make it the גוי's שחיטה, and the Jew can brush him off.

keyTerms.meaning: We look and see (it depends on the situation)
A violent, forceful person
Push away, refuse
Forbidden
"Your head and a mountain", a sharp brush-off

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי אליעזר, a small share counts only when the Jew cannot refuse it, such as with a violent גוי.

phrases.english: He said to him: We look at the situation.
If he is a violent man
whom [the Jew] cannot push away, it is forbidden.
And if not,
he can say to him: "Your head and a mountain!"
phrases.notes: Like saying "go bang your head on a mountain." The Jew just turns him down.

steps.triggerLanguage: חָזֵינַן, אִי אִינִישׁ אַלָּמָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Forbidden only if the גוי is violent and the Jew cannot refuse him. Otherwise the Jew sends him away and the coin does not matter.

steps.title: Slaughtering for mountains, seas and rivers is invalid
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: one who slaughters for the sake of mountains, hills, seas, rivers or wildernesses has an invalid שחיטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: one who slaughters for the sake of mountains, hills, seas, rivers or wildernesses, his שחיטה is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules that slaughtering in honor of parts of nature makes the שחיטה פסול.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the slaughterer himself has the wrong intention, slaughtering to honor mountains, seas and the like. Because his own intention is a form of worship, the שחיטה is invalid.

keyTerms.meaning: משנה, the start of a new משנה
For the sake of, in honor of
His slaughter is invalid
Hills

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who slaughters for the sake of mountains, for the sake of hills,
for the sake of seas, for the sake of rivers,
for the sake of wildernesses,
his slaughter is invalid.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשּׁוֹחֵט לְשֵׁם הָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Slaughtering for the sake of mountains, hills, seas, rivers or wildernesses makes the שחיטה פסולה.
